course.title: Baby First Health Early Childhood Development Certificate

module.title: Cognitive Development

target_learners.raw: Parents, caregivers, childcare workers, teachers, health practitioners, and anyone working with children aged 0–5.

learning_objectives: Understand how children aged 0–5 think and learn
Understand how everyday interactions, play, language, routines and safe exploration support learning

outline.title: The Role of Language and Interaction

blocks.text: A baby repeatedly drops a spoon from a high chair. An adult may feel tired of picking it up, but the baby may be learning something important: “When I let go, the spoon falls. It makes a sound. Someone picks it up. If I do it again, will the same thing happen?”

This is cognitive development in action. Young children are not empty containers waiting to be filled with information. From birth, they observe, listen, touch, repeat, test ideas, and try to understand the world around them.
By the end of this module, you will understand how children aged 0–5 think and learn, and how everyday interactions, play, language, routines, and safe exploration can support their learning.
items: Understand how children aged 0–5 think and learn
Understand how everyday interactions, play, language, routines and safe exploration support learning

blocks.text: Cognitive development means the way a child learns to think, understand, remember, pay attention, solve problems, and make sense of the world.

items: Remembering people, places, objects, and routines

blocks.text: Cognitive development is closely connected with physical development, language, emotions, and relationships. A child who feels safe, loved, healthy, and well nourished is better able to explore, concentrate, and learn.

WHO describes early learning as any opportunity for a child to interact with a person, place, or object in their environment. Every interaction contributes to brain development and lays a foundation for later learning.

blocks.title: Growth and thinking
blocks.text: A child may grow taller, but cognitive development is seen when the child:
items: Looks for a toy hidden under a cloth
Understands that a cup is for drinking
Pretends a banana is a telephone

blocks.text: Babies are active learners from birth. They learn through their senses—seeing, hearing, touching, tasting, smelling, and moving.

items: Talk, sing, and make eye contact
Respond to cries, smiles, gestures, and sounds
Repeat familiar songs, names, and routines
Play simple games such as peek-a-boo

blocks.text: WHO calls this responsive caregiving: noticing, understanding, and responding to a child’s signals in a timely and appropriate way. Responsive care supports health, nutrition, safety, learning, and emotional security.

blocks.title: Everyday examples
items: During feeding, a mother looks into her baby’s eyes, smiles, and says, “You are drinking your milk.”
A father shakes a plastic bottle filled with dry beans, and the baby listens, watches, and reaches for it.
A grandmother repeatedly calls the baby’s name during bathing, and the baby begins to turn toward the familiar voice.
A baby drops a spoon again and again. The caregiver calmly says, “The spoon fell down,” then gives it back. The baby is learning about falling, sound, and repetition.

blocks.text: CDC guidance notes that babies learn through play and interaction, including talking, reading, singing, peek-a-boo, and safe exploration.
Children develop cognitive skills at different rates. The patterns below are general guides, not deadlines or examinations.

blocks.label: 0–12 months
blocks.summary: Babies learn mainly through their senses, movement, and relationships.
learning_experiences: Looking at faces and following moving objects
Putting safe objects in the mouth to explore them
Learning cause and effect, such as shaking a rattle to make a sound
Looking for a partly hidden toy

notes.text: By around one year, many children explore objects by shaking, banging, throwing, putting things into containers, and taking them out. They may also copy gestures and follow simple directions.

blocks.label: 1–2 years
blocks.summary: Toddlers become curious explorers and begin to solve simple problems.
learning_experiences: Understanding what familiar objects are used for
Beginning pretend play, such as feeding a doll

notes.text: At around 18 months, many children know what ordinary objects are for, such as a spoon, brush, or telephone, and begin simple pretend play.

blocks.label: 2–3 years
blocks.summary: Children’s memory, language, and imagination grow quickly.

notes.text: By age two, many children can find objects hidden under two or three covers, begin sorting shapes and colours, and play simple make-believe games.

blocks.label: 3–5 years
blocks.summary: Preschool children become more thoughtful, imaginative, and independent.
learning_experiences: Counting and beginning to understand numbers
Solving simple problems with growing independence

notes.text: By age four, many children understand the idea of counting, remember parts of a story, and understand “same” and “different.” By age five, many can count objects, draw a person with several body parts, and tell a simple story.

items.text: Attention means the ability to focus on something.
Memory means the ability to keep and recall information.

blocks.text: Young children naturally have short attention spans. This is normal. A toddler may focus on a puzzle for a short time, then move to another activity. This does not mean the child is lazy or badly behaved.
Attention improves gradually as children grow, especially when activities are interesting, playful, and suited to their age.

items.label: Repetition
items.text: Singing the same song, reading the same story, or repeating a child’s name helps learning.

items.label: Routines
items.text: Regular meal, bath, play, and sleep routines help children predict what comes next.

items.label: Conversation
items.text: Talking about what happened during the day helps children remember events.

items.label: Songs and rhymes
items.text: Rhythm and repetition make information easier to remember.

items.label: Stories
items.text: Stories build listening, memory, imagination, and language.

items.label: Hands-on play
items.text: Children remember more when they can touch, move, build, sort, and explore.

blocks.text: A caregiver can sing the same simple hand-washing song each day. Over time, the child begins to remember the steps: wet hands, use soap, rub hands, rinse.
Do not expect every child to concentrate for the same length of time. Follow the child’s interest and keep learning activities short, enjoyable, and practical.
Young children ask questions, touch things, open containers, take objects apart, and repeat actions because they are learning.

items.text: Curiosity is the desire to know, see, try, or understand something.
Exploration is the child’s active effort to investigate the world.

blocks.intro: A child who opens every cupboard is not necessarily being naughty. The child may be learning:
items: What adults allow and what adults stop

blocks.text: Safe exploration is essential for learning. WHO emphasizes that early learning happens when children use their senses, move, hear and use language, experience different places, interact with people, and explore objects.
Keep dangerous items out of reach: medicines, chemicals, sharp objects, matches, small objects that can cause choking, and hot items.

items: Create a safe play area with safe household objects.
Allow the child to touch, stack, pour, sort, and investigate.

blocks.text: If a child asks, “Why does water spill?” the caregiver can say, “Water moves and flows. Let us pour a little water from this cup into the bowl and watch.”
Problem-solving means finding a way to reach a goal or deal with a challenge.

blocks.intro: Children learn to solve problems gradually. They may:

blocks.title: Everyday examples
items: A baby reaches for a toy that is slightly out of reach and rolls closer to it.
A toddler tries to fit a round object into a square hole, then tries another hole.
A preschool child builds a tower, watches it fall, and tries a wider base the next time.
A child looks for a missing shoe under the bed, behind a chair, and inside a basket.

blocks.text: Adults should not solve every problem immediately. Give the child a little time to try. Offer encouragement and small hints rather than taking over.
Instead of saying, “Give it to me, I will do it,” a caregiver can say, “Try turning the lid this way. You are working hard. Do you want help now?”
This builds confidence, patience, persistence, and thinking skills.

Play is one of the most important ways young children learn. WHO defines play as voluntary, enjoyable activity that may be imaginative, social, or solitary, and may involve objects. Young children build and strengthen developmental skills through playful interactions with people and objects.

items.low_cost_examples: Blocks, plastic cups, empty cartons, small stones

items.what_it_supports: Imagination, memory, language, understanding daily life
items.low_cost_examples: Feeding a doll, cooking with empty pots, pretending to go to market
Sorting bottle caps by colour, matching socks, grouping leaves
Homemade picture puzzles from old cards or magazines
Paper, charcoal, pencil, crayons, sand drawing
Family stories, picture books, local folktales
Local songs, counting songs, action rhymes
Looking at leaves, insects, clouds, shapes, and sounds

blocks.text: Children do not need expensive toys. Safe household objects and homemade materials can provide rich learning opportunities. WHO/UNICEF guidance encourages caregivers to use common household objects and homemade toys, along with talking, singing, and book sharing.

lessons.title: The Role of Language and Interaction

blocks.text: Talking with children is one of the most powerful ways to support cognitive development. Language gives children words for objects, feelings, actions, and ideas.

items: Encouraging children to explain their ideas

blocks.text: While cooking, a caregiver can say, “I am washing the tomatoes. The tomato is red. Now I am cutting it. What colour is this one?”

This does not require special materials or a formal classroom. Everyday activities such as feeding, bathing, walking, cooking, farming, shopping, and travelling can become learning moments. WHO notes that early learning opportunities are present in daily life, including at home, childcare, worship places, health facilities, and markets.
A child’s environment strongly influences learning opportunities. This does not mean a family needs wealth or many toys. It means creating safe, warm, responsive, and stimulating daily experiences.

items.label: Safe exploration
items.text: A clean, safe space where the child can move, touch, and play.

items.label: Responsive adults
items.text: Adults who notice and respond to the child’s sounds, questions, and interests.

items.label: Books and stories
items.text: Reading, picture sharing, storytelling, and local stories.

items.label: Conversation
items.text: Talking with the child in the family language.

items.label: Play opportunities
items.text: Time for free play, pretend play, and active play.

items.label: Predictable routines
items.text: Regular meals, sleep, hygiene, and play routines.

items.label: Sleep
items.text: Enough sleep supports attention, memory, mood, and learning.

items.label: Nutrition
items.text: Good nutrition supports brain development, energy, and concentration.

items.label: Physical activity
items.text: Movement supports overall development and helps children learn through the body.

items.label: Reduced unnecessary screen exposure
items.text: Screens should not replace play, conversation, sleep, or physical activity.

items.label: Emotional security
items.text: A child who feels safe and loved is more able to explore and learn.

blocks.text: WHO’s Nurturing Care Framework identifies good health, adequate nutrition, responsive caregiving, opportunities for early learning, and safety and security as essential conditions for children to thrive.
Families with limited resources can still support learning through talking, singing, storytelling, household play materials, routines, affection, and safe exploration.
Screens are part of modern life, but they should not replace the real-world experiences that young children need most: play, movement, conversation, relationships, and exploration.

The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends avoiding screen media other than video-chatting for children younger than 18 months. For children aged 18–24 months, if families choose to introduce media, it should be high-quality and used together with an adult. For children aged 2–5 years, the AAP recommends limiting screen use to one hour or less per day of high-quality programming, with adult involvement.

blocks.title: AAP screen media recommendations by age

rows.recommendation: Avoid screen media other than video-chatting
If families choose to introduce media, it should be high-quality and used together with an adult
One hour or less per day of high-quality programming, with adult involvement

items: Watch or use screens with the child when possible.
Talk about what the child is seeing.
Avoid screens during meals and for about one hour before bedtime.
Do not use screens as the main way to calm a child.
Make sure screens do not replace sleep, active play, reading, or family interaction.

blocks.text: Screens are not automatically harmful, but passive or excessive use can reduce time for the interactions and activities that best support learning. The AAP emphasizes that young children learn best through hands-on exploration and social interaction with trusted caregivers.
Children develop cognitive skills at different rates. One child may start talking early, while another may become skilled at building, sorting, remembering, or solving problems earlier.
This variation is normal. Children also have different strengths. One child may love stories, another may enjoy building, and another may be very observant outdoors.
Avoid constantly comparing children with siblings, cousins, classmates, or neighbours’ children. Comparison can create unnecessary pressure and may make adults miss the child’s individual strengths.

However, normal variation does not mean every concern should be ignored. If a child is not making progress over time, has significant difficulty in everyday activities, or loses skills they previously had, a qualified professional should assess the child.
A developmental concern does not automatically mean something is wrong. One behaviour alone does not diagnose a condition.

blocks.intro: Speak with a doctor, nurse, or other qualified child-health or developmental professional if you notice:
items: The child is not making expected progress in learning, attention, or problem-solving over time.
The child has significant difficulty understanding simple instructions or participating in age-appropriate play.
The child does not respond to their name, familiar people, or everyday sounds.
The child has persistent difficulty paying attention, remembering, or learning through play.
The child loses skills they previously had.
The child seems unusually disconnected from people, objects, or play.
The parent or caregiver has a concern that continues or seems unusual.

blocks.text: CDC advises caregivers to act early if a child is missing milestones, has lost previously acquired skills, or if the caregiver has any concern, and to ask for developmental screening.
Developmental screening is a short, structured check used by trained professionals to decide whether a child may need a fuller assessment. It is not a diagnosis.

blocks.title: Case: Ngozi and her three-year-old daughter, Chiamaka

narrative.text: Ngozi lives in Enugu, Nigeria, with her three-year-old daughter, Chiamaka. Chiamaka asks many questions: “Why is the pot hot?” “Where does rain come from?” “Why does the fan turn?”

She also opens plastic containers, takes lids off bottles, empties baskets, and repeatedly tries to fit objects into other objects. Ngozi sometimes feels Chiamaka is being troublesome, especially when she is busy cooking.

narrative.intro: One afternoon, Ngozi decides to observe Chiamaka more closely. She notices that Chiamaka is not simply making a mess. She is:
items: Trying different lids on different containers
Asking what will happen when she pours water from one cup to another
Pretending to cook after watching Ngozi in the kitchen
Remembering the steps of a song she learned at church

narrative.text: Ngozi creates a safer learning space. She gives Chiamaka clean plastic containers, safe lids, cups, and a bowl of dry beans. She sits nearby and asks, “Which lid fits this container? What do you think will happen if we pour the beans into the cup?”
Chiamaka tries, spills a few beans, laughs, and tries again. Ngozi says, “You are finding the right lid. Well done for trying again.”
Ngozi still keeps dangerous items locked away and supervises closely. She also answers Chiamaka’s questions in simple words and encourages her to explain her ideas.

what_this_case_teaches.heading: What this case teaches
items: Curiosity and exploration are important parts of learning.
A child’s “messy” behaviour can be an opportunity for problem-solving.
Adults can turn everyday household objects into learning materials.
Questions should be welcomed, not discouraged.

items.question: Why might Chiamaka keep opening containers and fitting objects together?
items.model_answer: She may be exploring size, shape, cause and effect, and problem-solving. She is learning through repetition and hands-on play.

items.question: How did Ngozi turn a challenging behaviour into a learning opportunity?
items.model_answer: She observed Chiamaka, provided safe materials, asked open questions, and encouraged her to try again without shaming her.

items.question: What cognitive skills was Chiamaka practising?
items.model_answer: She was practising problem-solving, sorting, matching, memory, curiosity, language, and pretend play.

items.question: What should Ngozi do to keep the activity safe?
items.model_answer: She should supervise closely, remove choking hazards and sharp or harmful objects, and keep medicines, chemicals, and hot items out of reach.

items.question: When should Ngozi seek professional advice?
items.model_answer: If Chiamaka’s concerns persist, if she stops making progress, or if she loses skills she previously had, Ngozi should discuss this with a qualified health or developmental professional.

items.better_approach: Give the child time to try, then offer help only when needed
Answer simply and use questions as learning moments

items.mistake: Calling a child “slow” or “stubborn” when exploring
items.better_approach: Describe the behaviour positively: “You are curious” or “You are trying to understand how it works”
Focus on each child’s own progress and strengths
Keep activities short, playful, and suited to the child’s age
Calmly redirect, explain, and give safe alternatives

items.mistake: Giving no opportunity for simple choices
items.better_approach: Offer limited choices, such as “red cup or blue cup?”

items.mistake: Relying entirely on screens for entertainment or learning
items.better_approach: Balance any screen use with play, conversation, movement, and stories
Use safe household objects, stories, songs, and everyday activities

blocks.title: Think Like a Child
blocks.instructions: Choose a safe everyday object, such as a plastic cup, spoon, lid, empty container, leaf, stone, or piece of cloth.
blocks.open_questions_intro: Sit with the child and explore the object together. Ask open questions such as:
open_questions: What do you think this is?
What do you think it does?
What happens if we put it inside this container?
Can you find another way to use it?
What do you think will happen next?
How are these two objects the same or different?
blocks.guidance: Let the child touch, try, and explain their ideas. Do not rush to give the correct answer.
blocks.baby_adaptation: For babies, simplify the activity: show a safe object, name it, let the baby touch it, and describe what the baby is doing.

items.text: Cognitive development is the way children learn to think, remember, understand, and solve problems.
Babies are active learners from birth and learn through relationships, senses, movement, and repetition.
Responsive caregiving means noticing and responding appropriately to a child’s signals.
Attention and memory develop gradually; young children naturally have short attention spans.
Curiosity, questions, touching, and exploration are important parts of learning.
Children build problem-solving skills by trying, observing, repeating, and changing their approach.
Play is a powerful way for children to develop thinking, language, imagination, and confidence.
Talking, singing, storytelling, and reading support cognitive development in everyday life.
Children do not need expensive toys; safe household and local materials can support learning.
Persistent concerns, significant difficulties, or loss of previously learned skills should be discussed with a qualified professional.

questions.question: What does cognitive development mean?

options.text: Only physical growth
How children learn to think, understand, remember, and solve problems
Only learning to speak
Only learning at school

questions.explanation: Cognitive development includes attention, memory, understanding, problem-solving, and learning.

questions.question: A baby repeatedly drops a spoon from a high chair. What may the baby be learning?

options.text: Nothing; the baby is only being difficult
Cause and effect, sound, and repetition
How to read
How to cook

questions.explanation: Repeating an action helps babies learn what happens and test cause and effect.

questions.question: Which activity best supports a toddler’s problem-solving skills?

options.text: Watching television alone for a long time
Trying to fit objects into containers
Being told to sit quietly all day
Avoiding all questions

questions.explanation: Fitting objects into containers encourages trial, error, observation, and problem-solving.

questions.question: What is responsive caregiving?

options.text: Giving a child whatever they ask for immediately
Noticing, understanding, and responding appropriately to a child’s signals
Allowing a child to do anything without limits
Speaking only when a child cries

questions.explanation: Responsive caregiving means responding in a timely and appropriate way to the child’s needs and signals.

questions.question: Why is repetition helpful for young children?

options.text: It makes children tired
It helps them remember and understand through practice
It replaces the need for play
It guarantees a child will speak early

questions.explanation: Songs, routines, stories, and repeated actions help children learn and remember.

questions.question: A three-year-old asks many “why” questions. What is the best caregiver response?

options.text: Tell the child to stop asking questions
Punish the child for being troublesome
Answer simply and turn the question into a learning moment
Give the child a screen to keep them quiet

questions.explanation: Questions show curiosity. Simple answers and shared exploration support learning.

questions.question: Which is an example of pretend play?

options.text: Sleeping
Feeding a doll with an empty spoon
Crying
Running

questions.explanation: Pretend play uses imagination and helps children understand everyday life.

questions.question: For children aged 2–5 years, what does the American Academy of Pediatrics recommend for screen use?

options.text: Unlimited screen use
No screen use at all, including video calls
One hour or less per day of high-quality programming, ideally with an adult
Screens during every meal

questions.explanation: The AAP recommends limiting screen use for ages 2–5 to one hour or less daily of high-quality content, with adult involvement where possible.

questions.question: A parent notices that a child who previously could say several words has stopped using them. What should the parent do?

options.text: Wait several years without action
Assume it is definitely a specific disorder
Discuss the concern with a qualified healthcare professional and ask about developmental screening
Stop talking to the child

questions.explanation: Loss of previously learned skills is an important concern that should be assessed by a qualified professional.

questions.question: A family has few toys. What is the best way to support a child’s cognitive development?

options.text: Wait until the family can buy expensive educational toys
Use safe household objects, stories, songs, conversation, and everyday activities
Keep the child indoors and silent
Use television as the main teacher

questions.explanation: Learning does not require expensive materials. Safe household objects and responsive interaction can strongly support development.

terms.definition: The way a child learns to think, understand, remember, and solve problems.
The ability to focus on a person, object, activity, or idea.
The ability to keep and recall information, people, events, and routines.
Finding a way to deal with a challenge or reach a goal.
Actively investigating people, objects, places, and experiences.
The desire to know, try, see, or understand something.
Mental skills that help a child focus, remember, control impulses, and plan simple actions.
Play in which a child uses imagination, such as pretending a banana is a telephone.
A skill that most children can do by a certain age, used as a general guide rather than a strict deadline.
A brief, structured check by a trained professional to identify whether a child may need further assessment.

professional_note.title: Professional Note
paragraphs: This module provides educational information about cognitive development in early childhood. It does not diagnose developmental conditions, disabilities, or illnesses.

Children develop at different rates, and one difference from a milestone does not automatically mean something is wrong. However, parents and caregivers should speak with an appropriate qualified health or developmental professional if they have persistent concerns, notice significant difficulties in everyday functioning, or observe a child losing skills they previously had. Developmental screening and professional assessment are appropriate next steps when concerns exist.
Urgent medical concerns should receive appropriate medical attention without delay.
